title: Who Really Pays for Free Returns?

beats.narration: You order a jacket online. It arrives on a Tuesday.
beats.visual: Phone shows a jacket product card; 'Add to cart' turns to 'Ordered'; parcel arcs to a house; calendar pops: TUE

beats.narration: By Thursday, you've decided the sleeves are too short.
beats.visual: Calendar flips to THU; large jacket with short sleeves and dashed measure lines

beats.narration: So you send it back. The label is free. The refund shows up a few days later.
beats.visual: Parcel gets a RETURN label and slides back; refund notification on the phone

beats.narration: For you, the story ends there. For the jacket, it's just getting started.
beats.visual: 'Done, for you' check; whole home layout slides out left, route line starts

beats.narration: It will be scanned, trucked, sorted, inspected, and judged. And every one of those steps costs somebody something.
beats.visual: Parcel travels a 5-station route (scanner, truck, warehouse, magnifier, gear); qualitative red cost meter fills, NO amounts

beats.narration: So who actually pays for a free return?
beats.visual: Title card with tilted orange FREE badge
on_screen_text: Who really pays for FREE returns?

beats.narration: Start with the scale.
beats.visual: One box multiplies into a 120-box grid (zoom-out metaphor)

beats.narration: In October 2025, the National Retail Federation and Happy Returns, a returns company owned by UPS, published a report based on two surveys: one of shoppers, one of large American retailers.
beats.visual: Report document + two sample cards
on_screen_text: National Retail Federation & Happy Returns (owned by UPS) · published Oct 15, 2025
2,006 U.S. consumers who had returned an online purchase in the past 12 months
358 e-commerce professionals at large U.S. retailers ($500M+ revenue)

beats.narration: Those retailers estimated that about 15.8 percent of their sales would come back in 2025.
beats.visual: Donut fills to 15.8%
on_screen_text: of annual sales expected to be returned in 2025
Average estimate across surveyed retailers · projection, not a final count

beats.narration: Across the whole industry, the report projected $849.9 billion worth of returned merchandise.
beats.visual: Counter to $849.9B + NRF historical bars (2019-2025, 2023 omitted by NRF)
on_screen_text: NRF series. 2023 omitted by NRF (different method). *2025 = projection.

beats.narration: Online, the estimate was higher: about 19.3 percent of online sales.
beats.visual: Two horizontal bars: all retail vs online
on_screen_text: Roughly one in five online purchases, by retailers' own estimates.

beats.narration: Keep in mind what those numbers are. They measure the value of goods sent back, not the cost of processing them. And they're projections for the United States, not a final count.
beats.visual: Two cards separated by a red ≠; three caveat pills

beats.narration: Shoppers are paying attention. In the same report, 82 percent of consumers said free returns are an important consideration when shopping online.
beats.visual: 10x10 dot grid fills 82 dots
on_screen_text: say free returns are an important consideration when shopping online
Base: 2,006 U.S. shoppers who had returned an online purchase in the past year

beats.narration: And 57 percent said they had decided not to shop with a retailer after it started charging for returns.
beats.visual: Dot grid fills 57 dots (red)
on_screen_text: decided not to shop with a retailer after it started charging for returns

beats.narration: So retailers are caught between two pressures. Returns are expensive, and making them harder can push customers away.
beats.visual: Balance beam rocking between two cards

beats.narration: Let's follow the jacket. What comes next is one common path, not the only one.
beats.visual: Persistent route map draws: Home → Hand-off → Consolidation → Returns center → Inspection → Decision; parcel at Home
on_screen_text: ONE COMMON PATH — NOT THE ONLY ONE

beats.narration: Step one: the hand-off. Depending on the store, you might mail it, leave it with a carrier, or bring it to a counter, sometimes without a box or a label.
beats.visual: Three hand-off options pop in

beats.narration: In NRF's survey, more retailers offered box-free, label-free drop-offs in 2025 than a year earlier.
beats.visual: Bars 2024 vs 2025
on_screen_text: Retailers offering no-box, no-label returns to carriers

beats.narration: Step two: consolidation. Instead of shipping every item back on its own, some return networks pool many returns together and ship them in bulk.
beats.visual: Nine single parcels slide onto a pallet; truck leaves

beats.narration: Step three: a warehouse or returns center, where someone opens the package and scans what's inside.
beats.visual: Warehouse; scanner beam over a parcel that opens; barcode

beats.narration: Step four: inspection. Is it the right item? Is it damaged? Has it been worn? Are the tags still on?
beats.visual: Magnifier over jacket; checklist ticks one by one

beats.narration: Step five: a decision. Restock it, discount it, send it somewhere else, or write it off.
beats.visual: Decision gear forks into four outcome boxes

beats.narration: This backward journey has a name: reverse logistics. And it can be slow. About half of the retailers in the NRF survey said it takes six to ten days to get a returned item back in stock.
beats.visual: Term reveal + ~49% figure and 10-day strip
on_screen_text: ~49% of retailers say it takes 6–10 days to get a returned item back in stock

beats.narration: All that time, the jacket isn't for sale. And if it's seasonal, it can lose value every week it sits.
beats.visual: Jacket with NOT FOR SALE tag; week counter; qualitative value bar shrinking
on_screen_text: resale value of a seasonal item
qualitative — the rate varies by product and season

beats.narration: So where does the money go? It helps to split the costs into two piles.
beats.visual: Two glass jars appear: red 'Operating costs' (left) and orange 'Lost value' (right)

beats.narration: The first pile is operating costs: money spent moving and handling the item.
beats.visual: Red jar glows; five illustrated stations fade in on a belt
on_screen_text: money spent moving and handling the item

beats.narration: Return shipping. Labor to receive, open, and inspect. Cleaning, repacking, or re-tagging. Customer service time. Software and fraud checks.
beats.visual: Returned parcel travels five stations (truck, workbench, repack, headset, fraud screen); a red coin flies into the jar at each spoken item

beats.narration: The second pile is lost value: what the item itself is no longer worth.
beats.visual: Orange jar glows
on_screen_text: what the item itself is no longer worth

beats.narration: A jacket that comes back in perfect shape, while it's still in season, might be resold at full price. One that comes back late, missing tags, or slightly worn may have to be marked down, or sold off in bulk for a fraction of its price.
beats.visual: Green jacket slides onto the FULL PRICE rail; a worn jacket gets a −% tag and drops onto a bulk pallet; orange coins fall into the lost-value jar

beats.narration: Here's a simple way to picture it. This is an illustrative example, not industry data.
beats.visual: Banner appears and stays for the whole example; jars empty

beats.narration: Imagine a jacket that sold for $100. Say the return shipping costs the seller $8, handling costs another $6, and because it's now out of season, it resells for $70.
beats.visual: Jacket with a $100 tag; coins '8' and '6' fly to the red jar as spoken; tag flips to $70 and a '30' coin flies to the orange jar

beats.narration: The customer got a full refund. The seller spent $14 to get back an item now worth $30 less. In this example, the seller is down $44 on a single return.
beats.visual: Jar totals pop as spoken ($14, $30); total banner

beats.narration: Change any assumption and the answer changes. Real costs depend on the product, the carrier contract, the warehouse, and the condition of the item.
beats.visual: Four dials turning
on_screen_text: Change an assumption, change the answer

beats.narration: There's also fraud. In the NRF survey, retailers that track it estimated that about 9 percent of returns were fraudulent, from empty boxes to swapped items. That's the retailers' own estimate, not an audited number.
beats.visual: 100 boxes, 9 turn red at the word 'nine'
on_screen_text: of returns, from empty boxes to swapped items
Self-reported by retailers that track it · not audited · illustration shows 9 in 100

beats.narration: So, who pays? The honest answer is: it depends on who's in the chain.
beats.visual: Money-flow stage: RETURN parcel in the centre, four actors (Retailer, Marketplace, Logistics partner, Shopper)
on_screen_text: It depends on who's in the chain.
the cost of a free return

beats.narration: Case one: a retailer selling its own products. Here, the retailer typically absorbs the cost of a free return directly, at least at first.
beats.visual: Coins stream from the parcel to the retailer, pile up there
on_screen_text: typically absorbs the cost directly, at least at first

beats.narration: Case two: a marketplace with independent sellers. The platform's rules decide how costs are split, and some marketplaces charge sellers fees tied to returns.
beats.visual: Coins go to the seller stall; one fee coin moves seller → platform
on_screen_text: platform rules split the cost; some charge sellers return-related fees

beats.narration: Amazon, for example, has charged returns processing fees on some products sold through its fulfillment service, under rules that vary by category and have changed over time.
beats.visual: Same stage with example caption; source line
on_screen_text: Amazon has charged returns processing fees on some products in its fulfillment service; rules vary and change

beats.narration: Case three: logistics partners. Carriers and returns companies get paid for their work. They're not absorbing the cost; they're billing for it, under contracts the public rarely sees.
beats.visual: Invoice flies from the truck to the retailer; a coin goes back to the truck
on_screen_text: carriers and returns companies are paid for their work: they bill for it

beats.narration: Case four: the shopper. Not always through a fee on that return, but potentially through prices, shipping charges, or memberships that help cover returns across all customers. How much that happens varies, and it's hard to measure from the outside.
beats.visual: Dashed 'possible' coins travel shopper → retailer, labelled as spoken

beats.narration: And more retailers are charging shoppers directly. In the NRF survey, 72 percent of merchants said they had started charging for at least one return option in the past 12 months, up from 66 percent the year before.
beats.visual: Bars 66% → 72%, synced to the spoken numbers
on_screen_text: Merchants that started charging for at least one return option (past 12 months)

beats.narration: That can mean a fee on one return method while another stays free, which nudges shoppers toward the option that's cheaper for the retailer. The cost doesn't vanish. It gets routed.
beats.visual: Street: shopper, mailbox with FEE tag, store with FREE tag; parcels flow along the free route
on_screen_text: A fee on one method, another stays free
The cost doesn't vanish. It gets routed.

beats.narration: Back to the jacket. Once it's been inspected, where does it actually go?
beats.visual: Sorting floor: conveyor across the top, eight dim bays below; magnifier over the belt
on_screen_text: Possible outcomes. Shares vary by retailer and product.

beats.narration: If it's in sellable condition, it can go back into stock and be sold as new.
beats.visual: Parcel drops down the first chute; 'Sold as new' bay lights up

beats.narration: If it's been opened or isn't quite perfect, it may be resold as used or open-box, usually at a discount.
beats.visual: Second bay lights up with a −% tag

beats.narration: Some items are repaired first. Others are sold in bulk to liquidators, who move them through discount stores and secondary markets.
beats.visual: Repair and liquidation bays light up as spoken

beats.narration: A 2025 study in the Journal of Business Logistics noted that more than $800 billion of returned and excess inventory passes through secondary market channels each year.
beats.visual: Fact panel over the dimmed belt
on_screen_text: of returned and excess inventory moves through secondary-market channels each year

beats.narration: Items can also go back to the original seller, get donated, or be recycled.
beats.visual: Three more bays light up as spoken

beats.narration: Amazon, for one, says the vast majority of its returns are resold as new or used, and that items it can't resell may be donated or recycled. That's the company's own account, and it doesn't describe every retailer.
beats.visual: Company-statement panel
on_screen_text: Amazon says the vast majority of its returns are resold as new or used

beats.narration: And some returns are destroyed. There's no single figure for the whole industry. A 2024 briefing by the European Environment Agency estimated that in Europe, between 22 and 43 percent of returned clothing bought online may end up destroyed, based on limited data.
beats.visual: 'Destroyed' bay lights red; EEA range panel
on_screen_text: of returned clothing bought online in Europe may end up destroyed

beats.narration: Since July 2026, the European Union has banned large companies from destroying unsold clothing, accessories, and footwear, with some exceptions.
beats.visual: EU rule panel
on_screen_text: Large companies may not destroy unsold clothing, accessories & footwear

scenes.title: Why free can still be good business
scenes.chapter: Why free can still pay off

beats.narration: If returns cost this much, why offer them for free at all?
beats.visual: Rocking FREE tag
on_screen_text: Why offer free returns at all?

beats.narration: Because a generous return policy can sell more than it costs. A 2016 review in the Journal of Retailing, which pooled results from 21 studies, found that more lenient return policies increased purchases. They increased returns too, but by less.
beats.visual: Two arrows grow when 'purchases' and 'returns' are spoken (qualitative heights)
on_screen_text: More lenient return policies increased purchases
Arrow heights are qualitative, not effect sizes.

beats.narration: Free returns lower the risk of buying something you can't touch or try on. That builds trust, and trust can turn browsers into buyers.
beats.visual: Phone with 'Free returns' + three-step chain

beats.narration: But there are trade-offs. Lenient policies can encourage bracketing, ordering several sizes and keeping one, and in some cases, outright abuse.
beats.visual: Three jacket sizes; S and L fly back

beats.narration: So retailers tune the dials: return windows, fees for some methods, exchanges instead of refunds, better size guides, and fraud screening.
beats.visual: Five sliders moving

beats.narration: In the NRF survey, retailers that added return fees reported fewer returns and more exchanges. But many also reported more customer complaints, and some said they lost customers.
beats.visual: Upside / downside cards
on_screen_text: Retailers that added return fees reported…

beats.narration: There's no free lunch here. Just a business decision about which costs are worth paying.
beats.visual: Balance with COST and SALES tags
on_screen_text: No free lunch. Just a business decision.

beats.narration: So, who really pays for free returns?
beats.visual: Title

beats.narration: Sometimes the retailer, out of its margin. Sometimes the seller, through marketplace fees. Sometimes the shopper, through fees on certain return methods, or possibly through prices. And part of the cost shows up as lost value, or waste.
beats.visual: RETURN box splits into four payer cards that appear as each is named
on_screen_text: Shopper — fees on some methods, possibly prices

beats.narration: What's almost never true is that the cost simply disappears. Someone decides how to absorb it, share it, or pass it along.
beats.visual: Flows thicken to all four
on_screen_text: The cost doesn't disappear. Someone decides where it goes.

beats.narration: So the next time you see free returns, read it as: free for you, at that moment.
beats.visual: FREE badge gains an asterisk

beats.narration: What would you trade for an easier return: a higher price, a shorter window, or a trip to the store?
beats.visual: Three answer cards appear as spoken
on_screen_text: What would you trade for an easier return?
